title: VagResist
text:
INSPIRE VAGINAL RESISTOME ANALYSIS


This website presents computational resources developed from the analysis of the vaginal resistome of the InSPIRe cohort (PRJEB77434). It also provides interactive access to the supplementary figures, tables, and data associated with this study.







RESOURCES





01 WORKFLOW


MoonCrater


A shotgun metagenomic workflow for antibiotic resistance gene read-count profiling.


 View on GitHub 





02 METRIC


PRD Index


The Phenotypic Resistance Diversity Index (PRDI) is a functionally informed diversity metric that integrates the predicted resistance phenotypes associated with acquired antimicrobial resistance genes.


 Calculate PRDI 





03 STUDY


InSPIRe Vaginal Resistome supplementary materials


Here you can interactively visualize the supplementary figures, tables, and datasets associated with the study.


Visualize









ASSOCIATED PUBLICATION


Boutouchent N, Baud A, Tazi A, et al. Bacterial community structure shapes the vaginal resistome during pregnancy. npj Biofilms and Microbiomes (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41522-026-01144-y

title: VagResist
text:
Supplementary Figure 1.




Supplementary Figure 1. Microbial composition of vaginal samples.


Taxonomic composition of all samples (n = 1,957) and of the subset collected at inclusion (IN; n = 1,045) and at delivery (DR; n = 912). The top 14 most abundant species are shown; all remaining species were grouped under “Other”.




Supplementary Figure 2.




Supplementary Figure 2. Transition frequency of dominant vaginal taxonomic profile between inclusion (IN) and delivery (DR) samples.


Heatmap showing the frequency of transitions in dominant species between IN and DR samples (n = 399 paired samples). Taxa were classified as dominant if they constituted ≥ 30 % of the profile. ‘other’ refers to the number of samples with a different dominant taxon. Rows represent the dominant species at inclusion, columns those at delivery. Values correspond to the number of individuals exhibiting a given transition. Color intensity is inversely related to transition frequency, with darker colors indicating lower frequencies. Statistical significance of inter-species differences in stability was assessed using a Monte Carlo permutation test on the χ² statistic.




Supplementary Figure 3.




Supplementary Figure 3. Cross-validation of antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) detection and diversity using CARD.


Relative abundance distribution of the top 10 ARGs (a) and corresponding antibiotic resistance classes (b) across all ARG-positive samples. (c) Prevalence and mean relative abundance of the top 20 ARGs detected using the CARD database. Each bubble represents one of the 20 most abundant ARGs: horizontal position shows mean relative abundance (log scale), bubble size reflects gene prevalence, and bubble color corresponds to antibiotic class.




Supplementary Figure 4.




Supplementary Figure 4. Extended phylogenetic projection of ARG-species associations in the vaginal microbiota.


A 16S rDNA-based tree of vaginal microbial species annotated with associated antibiotic resistance classes. Tree coloring indicates bacterial order (legend, upper right). For this representation, all species-ARG pairs within a single sample were displayed. ARGs (legend, left) are displayed along concentric arcs by antibiotic class.
View interactive tree on iTOL




Supplementary Figure 5.




Supplementary Figure 5. Cross-validation of antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) detection and diversity using an independent external cohort of pregnant women.


Visual comparison between the InSPIRe cohort and an external dataset (European Nucleotide Archive accession PRJEB34536) (left to right). Bubble plots show the 10 most abundant and prevalent ARGs, where bubble size represents prevalence and colors indicate antibiotic resistance classes (a, b). Panels (c, d) show the relative abundance of detected antibiotic resistance classes. Panels (e, f) show boxplots of the Shannon diversity index for ARGs across CSTs.

title: VagResist
text:
PRDI was calculated for both synthetical and biological samples as the total length of the branches of the smallest subtree connecting the observed ARGs to the root of the PhenoARGTree, following the Faith’s phylogenetic diversity formulation. This calculation was performed using the faith_pd () function from the scikit-bio library (v0.6.3).



PhenoARGTree


View interactive tree on iTOL



Conceptual validation of the PRDI was carried out using synthetic samples to distinguish between redundant augmentation of genes sharing the same resistance phenotype and “True” functional diversification. (addition of genes carrying distinct phenotypes). Starting with an initial subset of 50 randomly selected ARGs with unique phenotypes, the total number of genes was increased in increments of +5, +10, +20, +40, +80, and +100%, either by adding genes with the same phenotype (case 1: redundancy) or genes with new phenotypes (case 2: diversification). The α-diversity indices, including richness and Shannon, were calculated using scikit-bio (v0.6.3). The PRDI difference between the two cases as a function of the percentage added was modeled using the ordinary least squares method with robust standard errors (HC3).

Supplementary Figure 16.




Supplementary Figure 16. Distribution of human-filtered paired-end sequencing read depth across CSTs and clinical groups A–D.


Distribution of human-filtered paired-end sequencing read depth across CSTs (a) and clinical groups A–D (b). The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3), with the median indicated by an orange line. Whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR). Global differences across groups were assessed using the Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Dunn’s post hoc test for pairwise comparisons. Significant contrasts are indicated by red asterisks (p < 0.05). Analyses were performed at the sample level for descriptive comparison of sequencing depth distributions.

The color scale indicates the magnitude and direction of the size effect (positive values in brown for enrichment, negative values in blue for depletion). The x-axis shows dissimilarity values ranging from 0 (completely similar) to 1 (completely dissimilar), while the y-axis represents the density of sample pairs at a given dissimilarity value.

Supplementary figures 19. Distribution of human-filtered paired-end sequencing read depth across all samples.


The box extends from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3) of the data, with an orange line at the median. The whiskers extend to the point 1.5 times the interquartile range (IQR) from the box.

text:
Supplementary Figure 6.




Supplementary Figure 6. Composition of microbial taxa, ARGs, and MGEs across vaginal CSTs.


Relative abundance of microbial taxa (a), antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) (b), and mobile genetic element (MGE) families (c) across community state types (CSTs).




Supplementary Figure 7.




Supplementary Figure 7. Composition of microbial taxa, ARGs, and MGEs across vaginal CSTs.


Heatmaps of MaAsLin2 effect sizes for (a) microbial species, (b) antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), (c) mobile genetic elements (MGEs) across CSTs, with CST I set as reference. All models included patient ID as a random effect to account for repeated sampling. The color scale indicates the magnitude and direction of the effect size (positive values in brown for enrichment, negative values in blue for depletion). Significant results were annotated with an asterisk mark ( for an adjusted p-value < 0.1; and ** for adjusted p-value < 0.05).*




Supplementary Figure 8.




Supplementary Figure 8. Paired-samples comparisons of α-diversity for ARGs and MGEs across CST.


Each panel shows patient-matched diversity metrics comparing samples transitioning between community state types (CSTs): from CST I (a–c) or from CSTs I, II or V to CST III or IV (d–f). Lines connect values from the same individual. α-diversity metrics: observed richness (a, d), Shannon index (b, e), and Simpson index (c, f). Panels g–i and j–l depicts the same comparisons for mobile genetic elements (MGEs).




Supplementary Figure 9.




Supplementary Figure 9. Correlation network of the most abundant taxa, ARGs and MGEs in the vaginal microbiome.


(a) Network of the 20 most abundant microbial species and 50 clinically relevant antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). (b) Network including the same 20 microbial species, 50 ARGs, and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Nodes represent microbial species (blue), ARGs (pink), and MGEs (orange), with node size scaled by average relative abundance (%). Edges indicate significant correlations: blue edges represent positive correlations (ρ > 0.2, P < 0.01), and orange edges represent negative correlations (ρ < –0.2, P < 0.01); edge thickness is proportional to correlation strength.




Supplementary Figure 10.




Supplementary Figure 10. Co-abundance network of microbial species, antibiotic resistance genes (ARG), and mobile genetic elements (MGE).


(a) Network constructed from the 20 most abundant microbial species and 50 most prevalent clinically relevant ARGs. (b) Network including the same species and ARGs with the addition of MGEs. Nodes represent species, ARGs or MGEs, sized according to their average relative abundance. Edges indicate significant positive correlations filtered to display associations with p < 0.01 and ρ > 0.5; edge thickness is proportional to correlation strength. Communities were detected using the Louvain algorithm; node and edge colors indicate Resistance Co-Abundance Modules (RCAMs).




Supplementary Figure 11.




Supplementary Figure 11. Co-abundance network of microbial species, antibiotic resistance genes (ARG), and mobile genetic elements (MGE).


Network constructed from the 200 most abundant microbial species and most prevalent ARGs. Nodes represent species or ARGs. Edges indicate significant correlations (|ρ|> 0.4 and p < 0.01), with edge thickness proportional to correlation strength. Communities were identified using the Louvain algorithm, and node and edge colors indicate the corresponding modules.




Supplementary Figure 12.




Supplementary Figure 12. Association matrices between microbial species, ARGs, and MGEs generated using SparCC.


(a) SparCC-based correlation matrix between microbial species and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). (b) SparCC-based correlation matrix between microbial species and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Each matrix was hierarchically clustered using the clustermap() function from the Seaborn library with “average” linkage method.
